sections.section_heading: <<NOTE: 10 USC 2305 note.>> ENHANCED POST-AWARD DEBRIEFING RIGHTS.

dependencies.explanation: 10 U.S.C. 2305(b)(5) outlines post-award debriefing requirements for unsuccessful offerors in DoD procurements. Subparagraph (D) protects confidential and proprietary information of other offerors. The NDAA section directs revision of DFARS to strengthen these protections, mandates disclosure of agency source selection award determination (redacted) for high-value contracts, and requires written or oral debriefings for contracts over $10 million, ensuring both winning and losing offerors receive relevant information.

The NDAA section amends 10 U.S.C. 2305(b)(5) to allow disappointed offerors to submit follow-up questions within two business days after a post-award debriefing, requires agencies to respond in writing within five business days, and provides that the debriefing is not considered concluded until these responses are delivered. This expands the debriefing process and offers greater transparency and engagement for unsuccessful offerors.

31 U.S.C. 3553(d)(4) establishes timeframes for when contract performance can begin after a protest period. The NDAA amends this for DoD contracts, specifying that the 5-day post-debriefing protest period does not start until the government delivers written responses to follow-up questions submitted by disappointed offerors under the new 10 U.S.C. 2305(b)(5)(B)(vii) provision. This change links the protest timing to the expanded debriefing process.

sections.section_heading: LIMITATION ON UNILATERAL DEFINITIZATION.

dependencies.explanation: 10 U.S.C. 2326 establishes restrictions and requirements for undefinitized contractual actions (UCAs) in defense contracting, including deadlines for reaching agreement, limits on fund obligations, and oversight. Section 815 amends 2326 by: (1) adding a new subsection (c) that prohibits contracting officers from unilaterally finalizing contract terms, specifications, or price for UCAs over $50 million without written approval from the service acquisition executive or the Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition and Sustainment, notification to the contractor, and a 30-day waiting period; (2) redesignating existing subsections (c) through (i) as (d) through (j); and (3) updating subsection (b)(3) to reference 'subsection (h)' instead of 'subsection (g)' due to the new subsection.

sections.section_heading: SUNSET OF CERTAIN PROVISIONS RELATING TO THE PROCUREMENT OF GOODS OTHER THAN UNITED STATES GOODS.

dependencies.explanation: 10 U.S.C. 2534(c) sets limitations and sunset dates for procurement requirements concerning certain goods by the Department of Defense, including chemical weapons antidotes. This NDAA section adds a new paragraph (c)(5), causing the procurement restrictions concerning chemical weapons antidotes under subsections (a)(2) and (b)(2) to expire on October 1, 2018. After that date, domestic source limitations for chemical weapons antidotes are no longer effective.

dependencies.reference: section 858 of the Carl Levin and Howard P. 'Buck' McKeon National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2015 (Public Law 113-291; 10 U.S.C. 2534 note)
dependencies.explanation: Section 858 of the FY2015 NDAA required photovoltaic devices installed via Department of Defense contracts in the U.S. to be made in the U.S. from domestic materials, subject to exceptions. This NDAA section repeals that requirement effective October 1, 2018, thereby ending the domestic manufacturing requirement for photovoltaic devices procured under covered DoD contracts.

sections.section_heading: <<NOTE: 10 USC 2302 note.>> STATEMENTS OF PURPOSE FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENSE ACQUISITION.

dependencies.reference: Section 2545 of title 10, United States Code
dependencies.explanation: Section 2545 defines the 'defense acquisition system' as the workforce, management, and statutory/regulatory framework involved in DoD acquisition. The NDAA section uses this definition to clarify the scope for new statements of purpose in DFARS, but does not change the definition itself.

dependencies.reference: Section 108 of the National Security Act of 1947 (50 U.S.C. 3043)
dependencies.explanation: Section 3043 requires the President to submit an annual national security strategy report to Congress. The NDAA section references this to connect the DoD acquisition system's purpose to supporting national security strategy, but does not amend or alter section 3043.

sections.section_heading: EXPANSION OF DEFINITION OF COMPETITIVE PROCEDURES TO INCLUDE COMPETITIVE SELECTION FOR AWARD OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY PROPOSALS.

dependencies.reference: Section 2302(2)(B) of title 10, United States Code
dependencies.explanation: Section 2302(2)(B) defined 'competitive procedures' to include the competitive selection for award of basic research proposals. This NDAA section amends that definition by striking 'basic research' and inserting 'science and technology', thus expanding the scope to cover a broader range of research and technology proposal awards as competitive procedures in Defense procurement.

sections.section_heading: SCOPE OF REVIEW BY PROCUREMENT CENTER REPRESENTATIVES.

dependencies.explanation: This section defines the role and authorities of procurement center representatives in federal contracting. The NDAA adds a new paragraph (9) prohibiting the Administrator from limiting the scope of review by procurement center representatives for most contract/task order solicitations, and requires the Administrator to limit such reviews for certain Department of Defense solicitations (described in new (B)), unless the contracting agency requests review.

This subsection sets requirements for federal agency small business contracting goals. The NDAA adds a sentence clarifying that contracts excluded from procurement center representative review under subsection (l)(9)(B) must not be included when the agency establishes these goals.

Section 2762 authorizes Department of Defense contracts for sales to foreign countries under the Arms Export Control Act. The NDAA amends the Small Business Act to require that procurement center representatives' reviews be limited for DoD solicitations conducted under this authority unless specifically requested by the contracting agency.

Section 401 defines 'humanitarian operation' in the context of military humanitarian and civic assistance. The NDAA specifies that procurement center representatives' reviews are to be limited for DoD solicitations for humanitarian operations as defined here, unless the agency requests a review.

Section 101(a)(13) defines 'contingency operation' as military actions designated by the Secretary of Defense. The NDAA amends the Small Business Act to require that procurement center representatives' review is limited for DoD solicitations for contingency operations unless the agency requests review.

sections.section_heading: <<NOTE: 10 USC 2241 note.>> PROHIBITION ON USE OF FUNDS FOR CERTAIN PROGRAMS AND PROJECTS OF THE DEPARTMENT OF DEFENSE IN AFGHANISTAN THAT CANNOT BE SAFELY ACCESSED BY UNITED STATES GOVERNMENT PERSONNEL.

dependencies.reference: the date of the enactment of this Act
dependencies.explanation: Refers to the date the NDAA for Fiscal Year 2017 (Public Law 114-328) was enacted, which is December 23, 2016. The prohibition on obligating or expending funds applies only to programs or projects initiated on or after this date.

This NDAA section creates a new provision as a note under 10 U.S.C. 2241 concerning Department of Defense funding restrictions. It does not alter the existing text of 10 U.S.C. 2241 itself, but provides an additional restriction: DOD cannot fund Afghanistan programs/projects unless U.S. oversight can be safely conducted, with waivers and notification requirements.

sections.section_heading: <<NOTE: 10 USC 2305 note.>> REQUIREMENT AND REVIEW RELATING TO USE OF BRAND NAMES OR BRAND- NAME OR EQUIVALENT DESCRIPTIONS IN SOLICITATIONS.

dependencies.reference: section 2304(f) of title 10, United States Code
dependencies.explanation: 10 USC 2304(f) requires written justification and approval at specified levels for the use of non-competitive (sole source or limited source) contracting procedures. This NDAA section extends this requirement to any DoD solicitation using brand names, brand-name or equivalent descriptions, or proprietary specifications/standards, establishing that a justification must be provided and approved per section 2304(f) for such specifications.

sections.section_heading: <<NOTE: 10 USC 2305 note.>> USE OF COMMERCIAL OR NON- GOVERNMENT STANDARDS IN LIEU OF MILITARY SPECIFICATIONS AND STANDARDS.

dependencies.explanation: The note to 10 U.S.C. § 2305 includes prior guidance on DoD acquisition practices, particularly regarding specifications and standards. This NDAA section reinforces and expands these acquisition reform directives, requiring DoD to use commercial or non-government standards in lieu of military ones unless impractical, update policies and training, revise DFARS to encourage these practices, and partner with industry in standards development and licensing.

DFARS governs defense procurement regulations. Section 875 requires the Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition, Technology, and Logistics to revise DFARS within 180 days to encourage contractors to propose commercial or non-government standards and practices, thus implementing acquisition reform within DoD procurement regulations.

sections.section_heading: <<NOTE: 10 USC 2334 note.>> REPEAL OF MAJOR AUTOMATED INFORMATION SYSTEMS PROVISIONS.

dependencies.reference: chapter 144A of title 10, United States Code
dependencies.explanation: Chapter 144A established statutory requirements and reporting rules for major automated information system (MAIS) programs in the Department of Defense, including definitions, reporting thresholds, and oversight procedures. This NDAA section repeals chapter 144A entirely, eliminating legal frameworks and reporting requirements specifically for MAIS programs.

dependencies.reference: the tables of chapters at the beginning of subtitle A of such title, and at the beginning of part IV of subtitle A
dependencies.explanation: These are the organizational tables in Title 10 that list chapters by name. This NDAA section removes the listing for chapter 144A in both tables, reflecting the repeal of that chapter.

dependencies.reference: section 2334(a)(2) of title 10, United States Code
dependencies.explanation: Section 2334(a)(2) established the Director of Cost Assessment and Program Evaluation's duty to provide cost estimation guidance for major defense acquisition programs and major automated information system programs. This NDAA section amends 2334(a)(2) by striking reference to 'major automated information system under chapter 144A,' so the explicit requirement for independent cost estimates no longer applies to MAIS programs.

Sections 2445a through 2445d make up the substantive text of chapter 144A: definitions, annual and quarterly reporting, notice and certification requirements, and treatment when a program overlaps with major defense acquisition. This NDAA section repeals all these statutory provisions.

sections.section_heading: PREFERENCE FOR PERFORMANCE-BASED CONTRACT PAYMENTS.

dependencies.reference: Section 2307(b) of title 10, United States Code
dependencies.explanation: Amends 10 USC 2307(b) to expressly prefer performance-based payments for contract financing, clarifies these payments depend only on performance outcomes (not incurred costs), ensures nontraditional and private contractors are eligible, requires only compliance with GAAP for accounting systems (no government-specific requirements), and prevents DCAA from auditing GAAP compliance. Reorganizes and expands this subsection to strengthen the push for performance-based payment methods.

Requires the Secretary of Defense to revise DFARS within 120 days to reflect the amended provisions in 10 USC 2307(b), ensuring timely regulatory adoption of the preference and criteria for performance-based payments established by this NDAA section.

sections.section_heading: TREATMENT OF INDEPENDENT RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT COSTS ON CERTAIN CONTRACTS.

dependencies.reference: Section 2372 of title 10, United States Code
dependencies.explanation: This section previously governed regulations for payment of independent research and development (IR&D) costs by DoD. The NDAA section replaces it entirely, clarifying regulations for reporting and allowability, adding requirements for information exchange between DoD and contractors, and specifying the effective date for these regulations.

dependencies.reference: Section 2324(l) of title 10, United States Code
dependencies.explanation: Defines 'covered contracts' for purposes of allowable costs under defense contracts. The NDAA section requires bid and proposal costs to be allowable as indirect expenses on such contracts, provided they are allocable, reasonable, and not otherwise unallowable under law or FAR.

dependencies.reference: Section 1705 of title 10, United States Code
dependencies.explanation: Establishes the Department of Defense Acquisition Workforce Development Fund. The NDAA section allows this fund to support the advisory panel established when DoD exceeds its goal for reimbursable bid and proposal costs.

dependencies.reference: Section 2313a of title 10, United States Code
dependencies.explanation: Requires an annual report from the Defense Contract Audit Agency. The NDAA section amends this report to add summaries, by dollar amount and percentage, of contractor indirect costs for IR&D and bid and proposal costs, effective October 1, 2018.

dependencies.reference: Table of sections at the beginning of chapter 139 of title 10
dependencies.explanation: The NDAA section updates the table of sections to reflect the new headings for section 2372 ('Independent research and development costs: allowable costs') and adds section 2372a ('Bid and proposal costs: allowable costs').

sections.section_heading: ENHANCED COMPETITION REQUIREMENTS.

dependencies.reference: Section 2306a of title 10, United States Code
dependencies.explanation: This section sets federal procurement requirements for cost or pricing data ('truth in negotiations'). The NDAA amendment clarifies that certified cost or pricing data must be submitted for contracts using procedures other than sealed-bid procedures that are only expected to receive one bid, narrows the competition exception to cases where there are at least two or more responsive and viable competing bids, and adds a new provision making the prime contractor responsible for determining whether a subcontract qualifies for the competition exception from cost/pricing data submission requirements.

sections.section_heading: <<NOTE: 10 USC 2304 note.>> COMPETITION FOR RELIGIOUS SERVICES CONTRACTS.

dependencies.explanation: 10 U.S.C. § 2304 sets general rules for competition in DoD contracting. This NDAA section adds a legal note to that statute clarifying that the Department of Defense cannot prevent non-profit organizations from competing for contracts related to religious services on U.S. military installations. The concrete effect is to strengthen openness and competition for these specific contracts by explicitly allowing non-profits to participate.

sections.section_heading: AMENDMENTS CONCERNING DETECTION AND AVOIDANCE OF COUNTERFEIT ELECTRONIC PARTS.

dependencies.reference: Section 818(c)(2)(B) of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2012 (Public Law 112-81; 10 U.S.C. 2302 note)
dependencies.explanation: This provision set out contractor responsibilities related to detection and avoidance of counterfeit electronic parts in defense contracts. The FY16 NDAA amends it by: (1) clarifying that avoidance pertains specifically to counterfeit 'electronic' parts; (2) specifying that cost allowability only applies to 'covered' items and referencing eligible acquisition per relevant regulations; (3) requiring contractors to act when they discover counterfeit electronic parts or suspect such parts, making explicit their duty to report and remediate when discovery occurs.

dependencies.reference: Section 818(c)(3)(D)(iii) of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2012 (Public Law 112-81; 10 U.S.C. 2302 note)
dependencies.explanation: This clause previously required only 'review and audit' of trusted supplier identification by Department officials. The FY16 NDAA changes it to require 'review, audit, and approval,' thereby expanding oversight to require formal approval in addition to review or audit for trusted suppliers chosen by contractors.

This note contains implementing provisions from the NDAA 2012 concerning policies for detection and avoidance of counterfeit electronic parts. The FY16 NDAA updates this note through amendments to contractor and trusted supplier rules, strengthening compliance and making targeted clarifications to responsibilities and oversight as reflected in the changes above.

sections.section_heading: AMENDMENT TO MENTOR-PROTEGE PROGRAM.

dependencies.reference: Section 831 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 1991 (Public Law 101-510; 104 Stat. 1607; 10 U.S.C. 2302 note)
dependencies.explanation: This established the DoD Mentor-Protégé Program. NDAA 2016 section 861 substantially revises this section: expands the program's purposes, conditions, eligibility definitions, reporting and review requirements, and extends expiration dates. The original text could not be retrieved (unresolved), so changes are based only on the NDAA 2016 instructions.

dependencies.reference: Small Business Act (15 U.S.C. 631 et seq.)
dependencies.explanation: The Small Business Act sets federal small business policy and definitions. The NDAA 2016 section clarifies references and cross-references this Act in the Mentor-Protégé Program, including explicit statutory citations.

dependencies.reference: Section 3(a) of the Small Business Act (15 U.S.C. 632(a)) and regulations promulgated pursuant thereto
dependencies.explanation: Section 3(a) defines 'small business concern.' The NDAA modifies Mentor-Protégé definitions by cross-referencing the broader statutory definition and removing regulatory references.

dependencies.reference: Section 8(d)(7) of the Small Business Act (15 U.S.C. 637(d)(7))
dependencies.explanation: This requires contractors to report annually on small business subcontracting. NDAA section 861 creates a detailed annual reporting requirement for mentor firms to be compliant with this provision, specifying new data categories.

dependencies.reference: Section 21 of the Small Business Act (15 U.S.C. 648)
dependencies.explanation: This authorizes Small Business Development Centers (SBDCs) to assist small businesses. NDAA section 861 requires mentors to report if protégés receive assistance from SBDCs as part of annual reporting.

dependencies.reference: Entities providing procurement technical assistance pursuant to chapter 142 of title 10, United States Code
dependencies.explanation: Chapter 142 authorizes Procurement Technical Assistance Centers. NDAA section 861 mandates mentor firms to report assistance obtained for protégés from these entities.

dependencies.reference: Historically Black colleges or universities or minority institutions of higher education
dependencies.explanation: No specific statute cited, but these institutions participate in DoD diversity programs. NDAA section 861 requires mentor firms to report if they secure assistance from such institutions for protégés.

dependencies.reference: Section 2302 of title 10, United States Code
dependencies.explanation: Section 2302 defines 'nontraditional defense contractor.' NDAA section 861 expands eligibility for the Mentor-Protégé Program to include such contractors and establishes criteria for small business eligibility.

dependencies.reference: Section 8501 of title 41, United States Code
dependencies.explanation: Section 8501 defines 'blind' and 'severely disabled individual' for procurement. NDAA section 861 updates and clarifies Mentor-Protégé definitions by cross-referencing these statutory terms.

dependencies.reference: Section 632(p) of title 15, United States Code
dependencies.explanation: This provides definitions for HUBZone small business concerns. NDAA section 861 corrects references in Mentor-Protégé definitions to ensure compliance with HUBZone status.

dependencies.reference: Chapter 142 of title 10, United States Code
dependencies.explanation: Repeats the reference for procurement technical assistance. NDAA section 861 requires reporting of such assistance from authorized programs.

dependencies.reference: Section 637 of title 15, United States Code
dependencies.explanation: Section 637 covers additional SBA powers including contracts to disadvantaged businesses. NDAA section 861 incorporates its reporting requirements into the Mentor-Protégé annual report.

sections.section_heading: AMENDMENTS TO OTHER TRANSACTION AUTHORITY.

dependencies.explanation: 10 U.S.C. 2371 allows DoD to carry out research projects using flexible 'other transactions' authority (outside standard contracts, grants, or cooperative agreements). NDAA 2016 Section 815 builds on this by adding section 2371b, which extends similar flexible authority to prototype projects, introducing specific thresholds, approvals, and oversight.

Section 2371a allows federally funded research centers to enter into cooperative research and development agreements. Section 815 inserts the new section 2371b after 2371a, establishing where prototype authority fits in the Code, but doesn't amend section 2371a's substance.

Section 815 amends the definition of 'nontraditional defense contractor' in 10 U.S.C. 2302(9), making it clear that eligible entities must not have performed DoD contracts subject to full federal cost accounting standards (41 U.S.C. 1502) for at least the previous year before a procurement or transaction solicitation. This ties eligibility to the expanded prototype authority.

41 U.S.C. 1702(c) defines senior procurement executives for federal agencies. The new section 2371b requires these officials to approve high-value prototype projects, without amending the original section; it uses the responsibilities as a control for prototype authority.

15 U.S.C. 632 defines 'small business concern.' Section 815 refers to this definition for participant eligibility in prototype projects under new section 2371b, using the Small Business Act thresholds and requirements.

10 U.S.C. 2304 establishes competition requirements for federal contracts. Section 815 (new section 2371b(f)) allows DoD to award follow-on production contracts or transactions from prototype agreements without competitive procedures, under specific conditions, overriding the usual requirements of section 2304 in those cases.

41 U.S.C. 1502 establishes Federal Cost Accounting Standards, governing contract cost accounting requirements. Section 815 uses this section (via reference in amended 2302(9)) as the standard for determining whether an entity is a 'nontraditional defense contractor.'

dependencies.reference: Section 845 of the NDAA for FY1994 (Public Law 103-160; 10 U.S.C. 2371 note)
dependencies.explanation: Section 815 repeals section 845, which previously authorized DoD to use other transactions for prototype projects. Transactions entered under the repealed section 845 remain in effect and must be modified as appropriate to reflect the new amendments. (Reference could not be resolved; instruction is clear from NDAA text.)

dependencies.reference: Section 1601(c)(1)(B) of the NDAA for FY2004 (Public Law 108-136; 10 U.S.C. 2358 note)
dependencies.explanation: Section 815 amends subparagraph (B) to reference both section 2371 and new section 2371b, ensuring technical correctness and reflecting the expanded prototype project authority for acquisition and procurement purposes.

Chapter 21 of title 41 contains procurement ethics requirements. Section 815 (new section 2371b(h)) ensures that prototype agreements using other transaction authority are subject to these same ethical standards.

sections.section_heading: APPLICABILITY OF COST AND PRICING DATA AND CERTIFICATION REQUIREMENTS.

dependencies.reference: Section 2306a(b)(1) of title 10, United States Code
dependencies.explanation: 10 U.S.C. 2306a(b)(1) provides exceptions to the requirement for certified cost or pricing data in defense contracts. This amendment adds a new exception (subparagraph D) to exempt the submission of cost and pricing data that relates to offset agreements for sales of weapon systems or defense items to foreign countries or firms, except for data that relates to work performed in such country or by such firm that is directly related to the item being purchased. This broadens the pricing data waiver for international offset agreements.

sections.section_heading: LIMITATIONS ON SUBCONTRACTING.

dependencies.reference: The Small Business Act (15 U.S.C. 631 et seq.)
dependencies.explanation: The Small Business Act sets policies and operational rules for federal support of small businesses, including eligibility for contracting programs and requirements. This section amends the Act by adding a new Section 46, establishing explicit limits on how much of a contract a covered small business concern can subcontract, as well as requirements for similarly situated entities and domestic manufacturing.

dependencies.reference: Section 47 (as redesignated by section 1641 of this subtitle)
dependencies.explanation: Section 1641 of the NDAA 2013 redesignated Section 45 of the Small Business Act as Section 47, and inserted a new section on mentor-protege programs. Here, the new limitations on subcontracting (Section 46) are placed just before the newly redesignated Section 47, changing the order and numbering in the statute.

These are provisions in the Small Business Act that authorize specific contracting programs: 8(a) (contracts for socially/economically disadvantaged small business concerns), 8(m) (women-owned small businesses), 15(a) (general small business contracting), 31 (HUBZone program, 15 U.S.C. 657a), and 36 (service-disabled veteran-owned small businesses, 15 U.S.C. 657f). This NDAA section establishes new limits on how much these covered small businesses can subcontract on contracts awarded under any of these authorities.

Section 1641 of NDAA 2013 establishes mentor-protege programs for small businesses and redesignates statutory sections of the Small Business Act. Its effect here is organizational, specifying where the new Section 46 should be inserted into the existing statute.
